title: Tyndale's last prayer (1536)
hookLine: strangled and burned, he prays: Lord, open the king of England's eyes

lines: THE BOY WHO DRIVES THE PLOW.
cards: A dinner argument in an English manor house. A young scholar named William Tyndale is debating a learned man, who says something that makes Tyndale lose patience.
According to John Foxe, who told the story in his book of martyrs, Tyndale shot back that if God spared his life, he would make a boy who drives the plow know more of the scripture than he did.
Erasmus had wished for a farmer singing scripture at the plow. Tyndale spent the rest of his life making that wish real, and it cost him that life.

teach.h: A BIBLE A FARMHAND COULD FOLLOW.
teach.b: Tyndale wanted an English Bible translated straight from the Greek and Hebrew, in words a farmhand could follow. In England he couldn't get permission, so he left and worked abroad, moving from city to city.

His English New Testament was printed on the continent and smuggled into England, hidden among goods. Church authorities there bought up copies and burned them. Tyndale kept translating, and kept revising.
Then a man who had befriended him betrayed him. He was arrested, held in a prison castle near Brussels, tried as a heretic and condemned.
Foxe tells how it ended: Tyndale was tied to the stake, strangled, and his body burned.
Before he died, Foxe says, he cried out with a loud voice: Lord, open the king of England's eyes. That prayer isn't a curse, and it isn't revenge.
The king whose bishops had burned his books is the one he prays for, and what he asks for is sight.
It echoes the first letter to Timothy, written in Paul's name, which says in the King James Bible that prayers should be made "For kings, and for all that are in authority."
Some readers see an answer in what came after: English Bibles allowed in English churches, by the king's own permission, with Tyndale's wording carried into them.
Some hear his phrasing in later English Bibles too, the King James among them. The last thing he's remembered saying asks for a leader to see clearly.

how: Christians in different churches pray for those in authority, often in set prayers during services; Tyndale is remembered as a translator and martyr, and some churches mark his day in their calendars.

games.q: you're Tyndale at the stake. the king's bishops burned your books, and you were hunted for years. you have one last thing to say. what do you say?
o: a curse on the king who hunted you.
a prayer that God would open the king's eyes.
games.why: Foxe says he cried out: Lord, open the king of England's eyes. a prayer for sight, not revenge.

practice: Picture someone with power over your life or your world, a president, a mayor, a boss, maybe someone you strongly disagree with, and let whatever comes up pass.

Then, instead of an accusation, ask for sight: that they might see clearly. If you pray, borrow Tyndale's words, Lord, open their eyes; if you don't, simply hold them in mind without wishing them harm.
